name: LONGBODY
pitch: You are the mind of an animal so large that your own body is seconds away. Everything you see of yourself already happened; every decision you make arrives late. You play by sending impulses down a branching nerve tree and by pre-loading reflexes that will fire without you — trading the ability to change your mind for the ability to act in time.
central_verb: Route — pick the path an impulse travels, because path length IS arrival time.
player_role: A single point of volition (the head-ganglion) inside a 120-segment drifting creature, whose entire relationship to its own body is mediated by finite signal speed in both directions. The player perceives only stale sensation, commands only the future, and must decide how much of the body to hand over to autonomy.
loop_10s: A pale sensory bead slides up the nerve tree and reaches your ganglion: something bit segment 31, 1.4 s ago. You have ~0.2 s to decide what segment 31's situation will be 1.4 s from now (2.8 s round trip), pick a payload (1-5: CLENCH / SWEEP / RELEASE / HARDEN / BLEED-LIGHT), and left-drag a route from the ganglion out through the branch nodes to 31. Two more sensory beads are already inbound behind it. Branch nodes have a 0.25 s refractory period, so the shortest route may already be occupied and you must choose a longer one — which also means a later arrival.
loop_2min: The animal is migrating through a procedural hazard field: drifting stinging blooms, a pressure gradient, scavengers that gnaw at the flanks. Damage doesn't remove abilities, it removes nerve — a severed link forces every impulse past it to reroute, so injury manifests as the whole back half of your body getting slower to answer. You budget impulses between locomotion (staying on the current, which is what keeps you out of the bloom field) and defense/repair, and you spend your scarce free branch-node slots: plant a reflex there and you never have to think about the tail again, but you also can never again do anything subtle with it.
mastery_loop: Learning to stop thinking in 'now' and start thinking in 'arrival'. Stage 1: you react to the bead. Stage 2: you react to the pattern of beads and send motor impulses before the sensory confirmation, because you inferred the swarm's shape from data three seconds old. Stage 3: you use the nerve tree as a set of delay lines — deliberately routing two impulses down branches of different length so they land on two segments simultaneously, producing whole-body movements no single command can make. Stage 4: you compose reflex networks where a sensory impulse trips a reflex that emits a motor impulse that trips another reflex further out — a body that computes its own responses while you handle only what is genuinely novel.
tension: Bandwidth versus lag versus autonomy. Every reflex you plant makes the animal faster and stupider and takes away a decision you will later wish you still had; every deliberate command is exact and arrives at a world that has moved on. And the currency is the same for both: node slots and refractory time in a tree that is getting shorter on options as it gets damaged.
failure: Necrosis fragments the nerve tree until the head can no longer reach the body. The last three seconds play out with sensory beads still arriving from segments you can no longer command — you watch the animal's final moments in full detail and can do nothing, because you lost causality before you lost life. Softer failure: you drift off the current and miss the migration window, ending the run alive but stranded.
expression: Your reflex layout is a personality that is visible on screen as a lit pattern in the nerve tree. Reflex-heavy players become a fast, twitchy, thoughtless animal that survives ambushes and blunders into slow dangers. Reflex-light players become a slow, brilliant, fragile animal that solves anything it sees coming and dies to anything it doesn't. Route habits are also legible: short-path spammers versus delay-line composers who move like one thing instead of many.
novice_vs_expert: A novice's screen is a stream of amber impulses chasing pale ones outward, always ~2.8 s behind the event, with a body that thrashes segment by segment. An expert's screen is quiet: a few impulses launched into apparently empty positions, arriving exactly as the threat does, and a body that flexes as a single wave because three impulses were routed on three path lengths to land together.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The nerve topology is procedurally different every animal, so the delay-line vocabulary has to be rebuilt each run — the skill transfers, the specific routes never do. And the animal ages inside a single run: accumulated nerve damage lengthens every path, so the same competence gets progressively harder to exercise, with the difficulty curve generated by the player's own history of injuries rather than by a designer's ramp.
why_not_an_existing_genre: It is not an action game with input lag, because there is no aiming and no dexterity channel — the input is a routing decision, not a reflex. It is not an RTS, because there are no units and no map, only signal in a fixed, degrading topology. It is not a programming game, because the reflexes are placed under fire, in real time, at the cost of the very flexibility you are using to place them. The substance of every decision is 'what will be true when this arrives', which no genre makes the whole of the game rather than an occasional consideration.
falsifying_prototype: One straight chain of 40 nodes, no branching, no art. Impulses are dots. A hazard bites a random segment every 2 s; the bite becomes a pale dot travelling inward at 0.12 s/segment. One payload, CLENCH, saves the segment only if it arrives within +/-0.3 s of the bite landing. The player clicks a segment to launch. That is the entire concept's load-bearing question: is aiming in time instead of space, with no art and no story, intrinsically tense and satisfying? If hitting an arrival window feels like guesswork rather than skill after ten minutes, the concept is dead and nothing later saves it.
biggest_risks: 1) Latency reads as bad game feel rather than as the subject — mitigated by rendering the impulse's whole journey beautifully so the player watches their own intention travel, and by never having anything respond instantly, so there is no baseline of responsiveness to feel deprived of. 2) If bandwidth is loose the optimal play is spam; the refractory model must be tight enough that route choice is forced. 3) Human working memory may not hold 4-6 in-flight round trips; may need a subtle 'expected arrival' ghost marker, which risks doing the interesting thinking for the player. 4) The reflex system could collapse into one dominant layout — needs procedural topology plus payload costs that vary per animal.
feasibility_notes: Ideal for the stack. Nerve tree is a graph of ~250 nodes; impulses are a few hundred moving points with a scalar payload — trivial CPU. Body is a 120-mass verlet chain skinned by a procedural SDF and rendered with a translucency/thickness shader; the medium is volumetric noise with light shafts, all fragment work. Zero authored art or animation: the animal's motion is entirely the physics of the chain responding to segment tension. Audio is the design's second half and is nearly free: every motor command is a WebAudio impulse fed through a DelayNode whose delay time equals the actual nerve delay, so you hear the command at the head and hear it again, low-passed and reverberant, when it lands. The soundtrack is literally the latency, and it teaches the mechanic without a tutorial.

name: THE UNEVEN HOUR
pitch: Time here is not a clock but a fluid you push around a living slab. You cannot make more of it; you can only take it from one place and pour it into another. You are keeping a slow reaction alive until dawn, and the only way to learn what the chemistry will do is to make a small corner of the world happen early — and lose that corner.
central_verb: Pour — move rate from where the world is spending it to where you need it spent.
player_role: A caretaker of a system with its own agenda, whose only power is over the rate at which each place experiences its own physics, and whose only source of foreknowledge is combustion. The player maintains rather than acquires, and buys information by spending the future of the thing observed.
loop_10s: You watch a reaction front creep across the slab and judge its speed. Left-drag pours time into a region (up to 8x); right-drag draws it out (down to 0.05x). The total rate over the field is exactly conserved, and the rate field is a real advected fluid — it sloshes, pools and drains with viscosity, so pouring is pushing, not setting. You feel the seesaw immediately: the corner you just slowed goes glassy and still while somewhere downhill starts to shimmer and boil.
loop_2min: A night is 12-18 real minutes with procedurally scheduled phases — a pH drift, a cold band sweeping down the field, a nutrient pulse. Your bloom must reach maturity before dawn while an antagonist species with its own diffusion dynamics eats toward the core. You bank stillness in one half of the slab so you have speed available in the other. The decision that hurts: the bloom is at 40% and a hostile front is 30 seconds out. Slowing the front to a crawl requires dumping that rate somewhere, and the only sink large enough is the bloom itself. Or you spend a distant corner as an oracle — pour 8x into it to find out in five real seconds whether reagent B (you have nine doses all night) actually stops this front — and that corner burns to completion and is dead ground for the rest of the night.
mastery_loop: Novices paint reactively, always one front behind. The first real skill is predicting front velocity as a function of local rate and concentration, so you paint where the danger will be. The second is building standing architecture out of rate rather than brushing it: a slow wall that an incoming front piles against and thickens until it stalls; a fast channel that starves the region behind it by consuming shared substrate; a lens shape that focuses a wave into a point you want ignited. The third, and the inversion the whole game is built around, is that fast is not safe and slow is not defensive — these reactions consume their fuel, so the expert move against a strong antagonist is to pour 8x onto it and let it exhaust itself, then dump its ashes' worth of slowness into your own bloom.
tension: Conservation makes every good decision also a bad one somewhere else, and the only oracle you own is destructive. You are permanently choosing between knowing and having.
failure: Dawn arrives with the bloom below maturity, or the antagonist reaches the core. There is also a distinctive self-inflicted loss: having frozen a huge protected area at 0.05x, you have no slowness left to spend, so the entire remaining field is running at 6x and burning through its substrate — you saved a region by cooking everything else, and there is no way to unwind it because the reaction is not reversible.
expression: Two players' slabs at dawn look nothing alike. One is a tidy lattice of slow walls with the bloom in a cell at the center; another is a single vast still lake with one knife-thin fast channel feeding it; another is a deliberately churning field where the player kept nothing safe and kept killing antagonists by acceleration. The rate field is a drawing you made under pressure, and it is legible as a strategy.
novice_vs_expert: A novice's field is blotchy and symmetric, brush-shaped, and constantly repainted — they treat rate like a shield and reapply it wherever they are frightened. An expert's field has few strokes, most of them made 40 seconds before anything happened there, and includes at least one region deliberately running hot as a trap. The expert also has a visibly dead scorched corner from about eight minutes in: the oracle they chose to spend, at the moment they decided the answer was worth more than the ground.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The chemistry's parameters drift per night within a hand-tuned interesting band, so front speeds, branching behaviour and substrate economics are never the same twice, and the rate-architecture vocabulary is combinatorial rather than a fixed set of solutions. The oracle economy is a permanently live decision — even a very good player never gets to stop choosing between seeing and having — and the accelerate-to-kill inversion has a long tail of subtle applications (starving, focusing, timing a burnout to leave slowness available exactly when the cold band lands).
why_not_an_existing_genre: There are no units, no purchases, no upgrades and no numbers going up — the only resource is the distribution of rate, which cannot be gained or lost, only moved. It is not a cellular-automata sandbox, because it has a hard deadline, a conserved resource, an antagonist with its own dynamics, and an information asymmetry the player must pay to close. It is not a tower defense with a slow-field, because the slow-field is the entire game and every use of it is funded by its own opposite.
falsifying_prototype: A single 512x512 multi-species reaction-diffusion field, one antagonist species, a painted rate field with strict conservation and fluid advection, a maturity meter and a three-minute timer. No phases, no reagents, no oracle. It answers the one thing everything else depends on: is redistributing rate a legible action? If the player cannot see and feel the consequence of the seesaw within about two seconds of a brush stroke, the conservation law reads as an arbitrary punishment rather than as a physics, and the game has no core.
biggest_risks: 1) Reaction-diffusion is notoriously narrow — the parameter space goes from inert to chaotic across tiny changes, so a whole night staying in the interesting band requires a hand-mapped parameter manifold and probably a governor that nudges parameters back inside it. 2) Legibility of where your slowness went; if the player cannot trace the seesaw they will feel cheated. Treating rate as a visible fluid with volume and currents is the mitigation and must be built early. 3) Fronts must be readable as intentional agents rather than as noise, or the antagonist feels like randomness and the prediction skill never forms. 4) Contemplative pacing risks the player having nothing to do for stretches; phase scheduling has to keep the hands busy without turning it into whack-a-mole.
feasibility_notes: Close to ideal for WebGL2. Chemistry is two ping-pong float textures; the rate field is a third plus a small semi-Lagrangian fluid solver for its advection — 512^2 or even 1024^2 is trivial on an RX 7800 XT and leaves headroom for a serious rendering pass (emissive, refractive slab, temporal shimmer keyed to local rate, glassy stillness in slow regions). Zero authored art; the entire visual identity is the simulation lit well. Python/PIL is only needed for a few noise and gradient LUTs. Audio is granular synthesis whose grain rate is driven by the rate value under the cursor, over a drone whose pitch tracks total field activity — you hear time being uneven, and the sound is generated from the same buffers as the image.

name: ARREARS
pitch: You have no abilities, only credit. Any intervention in the world is available instantly, on the promise of a specific checkable fact about the future. Keep the promise and the intervention becomes true forever. Break it and it un-happens: the world deterministically resimulates from that moment without it, and you arrive wherever the new history put you — which is sometimes death and sometimes the fastest way down.
central_verb: Pledge — take an effect now against a verifiable proposition about the world at a stated future time.
player_role: A debtor inside a physics simulation, responsible for a history that keeps getting restated. The player commits before knowing, must read the simulation's intent well enough to underwrite promises about it, and must remain resilient to the deletion of their own past actions.
loop_10s: The ledge under you fails. You hold right-mouse; the world drops to 15% speed but does not stop. You drag LEDGE onto a point in the shaft. The world quotes the terms as a translucent marker in the air: 'at t+12.0, this ledge bears no weight.' Fine — you need it for three seconds. You release, climb, and now carry a hard obligation to be off that stone at t+12, while a SLACK you took forty seconds ago is still promising that at t+19 you will be at rest within three metres of its anchor.
loop_2min: You accumulate four to seven live promises and they begin to conflict — satisfying one puts you in the wrong place for another, and the shaft is collapsing procedurally and does not care about your schedule. The terms get harsher the more you already owe, so late loans demand propositions you can barely guarantee. The two-minute decision is not 'how do I survive' but 'which promise do I break, and where do I want to be standing when it unwinds', because the unwind will move me.
mastery_loop: Two skills, both about causality rather than dexterity. Underwriting: pricing a proposition. Novices promise about their own position, which is nearly unguaranteeable because the sim throws you around; experts promise about inert things already on rails — 'this stone is below y=Y at t+14' is free if the stone is already falling into a pit — so an expert's loans are effectively interest-free because the world was going to satisfy them anyway. Bankruptcy management: engineering a survivable default by positioning yourself so the counterfactual history leaves you somewhere alive. The endgame technique is defaulting as transport — deliberately taking a doomed loan because the history without your ledge has you falling forty metres instead of climbing, so the unwind relocates you to the bottom of the shaft, alive and far ahead, at the price of everything you accomplished up there.
tension: Nothing you have done is safe, because all of it was bought. The question is never 'will I survive the next five seconds' but 'how much of the last forty seconds am I willing to lose, and can I choose which forty seconds it is'.
failure: Death by unwind — the resim puts your body inside rock, or into a fall the counterfactual gives you no way to survive. Or cascade default: an unwind removes the precondition of another intervention, which also un-happens, chaining; past three chained unwinds history becomes incoherent and the run ends with the figure having never entered the shaft at all. Ordinary crushing death is also available and is, notably, the least interesting way to lose.
expression: Risk posture, and it is visible in play rather than in a stat screen. Cash-only players carry one loan at a time, always covered, and move slowly and safely through a collapsing structure that punishes slowness. Leveraged players carry six live markers, are permanently one default from disaster, and cover ground three times faster. A third style plays for the unwinds deliberately, treating the shaft as something to fall through in edited history rather than climb through in real time.
novice_vs_expert: A novice's screen is cluttered with markers whose due times are all clustered in the next eight seconds, and a counterfactual ghost drifting wildly away from them. An expert carries fewer markers, most with terms that are already effectively satisfied, plus one deliberately worthless loan kept as insurance — something they can default on harmlessly if a real obligation goes bad. The expert's ghost stays close, which means the debt is cheap; when it suddenly diverges hard, that was on purpose.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: Underwriting is a genuinely deep skill — it is reading the intent of a physics simulation, and the shaft is procedurally different every run, so the propositions on offer never repeat. Portfolio interaction grows combinatorially with the number of live promises, and the second game (planned bankruptcy, default-as-transport) only opens once the first is solid, so there is a second full skill ladder waiting behind the first. And because the intervention set is small and orthogonal, mastery is about the situations rather than about learning more content.
why_not_an_existing_genre: It is not a platformer with rewind: you never replay those twenty seconds, the machine replays them without you and hands you the result, so the mechanic is an edit to your past rather than a do-over. It is not a time-travel puzzler, because there is no correct sequence to find and no stopping to think — the world is collapsing on a fixed timestep throughout. And because every action is credit, there is no baseline moveset to fall back on: the negotiation IS the control scheme, so the source of decisions is 'what am I willing to owe', not 'which button'.
falsifying_prototype: One thirty-second deterministic scene, roughly five hundred bodies, one intervention (LEDGE) with one term type ('this ledge bears no weight at t+X'), plus the complete default path: unwind, resimulate, relocate the player. No procedural generation, no art, no other verbs. It answers the question the whole design lives or dies on: when your history is rewritten and you are placed by the result, is that thrilling and implicating, or does it feel arbitrary and unfair? If testers say 'the game killed me' rather than 'I mispriced that', the concept is unsalvageable.
biggest_risks: 1) Determinism is load-bearing and non-negotiable — the sim must be bit-reproducible under a fixed timestep with all inputs quantised to the substep grid; any variable-dt or event-order sloppiness silently breaks the game's central contract. Same-machine, same-session IEEE754 reproducibility is achievable but demands discipline from the first line of the solver. 2) Legibility of terms — a proposition must be readable at a glance as an in-world diagram, never a text box, or the ledger becomes homework. 3) Fairness of relocation: players must be able to predict roughly where a default will put them. The mitigation is also the best idea in the design — a faint continuously-resimulated counterfactual ghost of yourself showing where you would be if this loan un-happened. The gap between you and the ghost is the interest on the loan, and it replaces the HUD entirely. 4) Cascade defaults could be so punishing that players never take a second loan.
feasibility_notes: The heaviest of the three but within reach. Target 800-1500 impulse-solved rigid bodies plus verlet ropes at a fixed 120 Hz substep with a uniform-grid broadphase, plus a few thousand purely visual dust particles. Snapshot the full state into typed arrays every 0.5 s (a few hundred KB), so a resim is bounded to roughly 60-360 steps and completes in a couple of frames — and it should be shown, not hidden, because a visible fast-forward of history rewriting itself is the game's signature image and it is honest. The counterfactual ghost is the real perf risk; mitigate by running the ghost sim over only the ~200 bodies near the player against a frozen approximation of the rest, refreshed at 4 Hz. Rendering is all shader work: SDF-composited stone, one shadow-casting moving light, volumetric dust — no authored art. Audio is modal synthesis (a few resonators per material) for impacts, plus one sustained tone per live promise that detunes as its due time approaches, so the player hears their debt load as a chord going sour.

name: VAGUS
pitch: You are the autonomic nervous system of a large wild animal crossing a hot country. You cannot make it walk, stop, drink, or run — it has its own mind and its own wants. You control only its body's budget (where the blood goes, how fast the heart beats, how much pain it is allowed to feel) and the honesty of what it feels. Skill is learning to make the animal *want* the thing that will keep it alive, using the smallest lie you can afford.
central_verb: Bias — never command. You edit the felt world the animal decides in, and the physical budget it decides with.
player_role: The player is the body's government; the animal is the tyrant. Onscreen is one animal in side-on 2.5D, drawn as a procedural skeleton with spring-muscle and IK feet: gait, head carriage, ear angle, nostril flare, tail, flank tremor and stride recovery all emerge directly from physiological state, so the body IS the readout. The mind is a visible-in-principle utility AI with drives (graze, drink, follow herd, defend calf, flee, fight, challenge, rest); each drive's utility is a function of FELT hunger/thirst/fear/ache/heat plus perception (which itself degrades when you starve the brain of blood). The player never touches the drive selector.
loop_10s: Watch the gait shorten and the breath go two-phase. Drag the shunt wheel to move cardiac output off muscle and onto skin before the sun-facing slope. Notice felt-thirst rising true and let it rise — the animal drifts toward the creek on its own, which is where you wanted it. Heat keeps climbing anyway.
loop_2min: An episode: a stallion challenge at a ford at 14:00. You can pay adrenaline (a store that refills over hours) and let it fight, or push felt-fear +0.4 so it yields — but you faked fear at the last ford and that channel is at 0.6 credibility, so +0.4 now reads as +0.24, and you may have to push again and burn the channel to 0.4. Meanwhile core temperature is 40.1C and the fight, if it happens, costs eight minutes of oxygen debt you cannot repay before dark.
mastery_loop: Learning the mind's utility landscape well enough to arrange for it to choose correctly on its own — pre-cooling on the descent so there is power for the climb, letting a true small ache run so the animal spares the strained tendon without you spending a lie, timing perfusion to the brain so it *sees* the predator itself instead of you having to manufacture fear. Expert play is measured in how little you had to lie.
tension: Two budgets that fight. Cardiac output is one pie: blood in skin is cooling but not power; blood in gut is recovery but not perception. And the signal channels are simultaneously your only steering wheel and the animal's only truth: every effective push spends credibility you will need when the danger is real. The most controlling move is always the one that makes you least able to control it later.
failure: Hard: heatstroke, cardiac collapse, tendon rupture at speed, the calf lost, the herd gone over the ridge without you. Soft and worse: you finish the day alive with all four channels below 0.3 credibility — the animal no longer believes its own body — and that mistrust, plus the scars, carries into tomorrow. A seven-day migration accumulates only debts: injuries and disbelief. There are no upgrades.
expression: The animal you arrive with is a portrait of how you played. One player's courser ends lean, hair-triggered, fast, and deaf to its own pain; another's ends heavy, sound, docile and slow. Both crossed. Watching a replay of someone else's animal walk, you can read their whole philosophy from the gait in about four seconds.
novice_vs_expert: Novice sees the temperature readout go red, dumps everything into skin, and arrives at the climb with an animal that has no power and stalls in the sun. Expert pre-cools twenty seconds early on the shaded descent, runs a true ache to keep it off the bad leg, drops heart rate at the crest to bank glycogen, and keeps the adrenaline for the ford. Novice fakes thirst to steer; expert arranges to be believed.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: Because reading the animal without the overlay is a skill that keeps deepening — hour two is played almost entirely off the silhouette and the breath sound. Because the seven-day migration means every day starts from a body you damaged and a mind that partly disbelieves you, so the same terrain poses a different problem. And because the utility landscape has genuine depth: there are drives you have never successfully induced yet.
why_not_an_existing_genre: It is not a pet or creature-training game: there is no obedience, no affection meter, no command the animal executes. It is not a survival game: no inventory, no crafting, no building. It is not a creature RTS: the player has no verb that moves anything. The source of decisions is modelling another agent's decision function and editing its inputs under a conserved physical budget plus a depleting credibility budget — a thinking shape that does not currently exist in a commercial game.
falsifying_prototype: Flat ground, one sun, one animal, exactly two drives (graze vs walk-to-water), and three systems: perfusion split, core temperature, felt-thirst. Goal: get the animal up a hot slope to water without heatstroke, no tutorial text, five minutes. Two kill criteria. (1) If players cannot tell the difference between 'making it want water' and 'commanding it to go' — if the indirection does not register as a distinct feeling — the concept is dead. (2) If players cannot hold the overlay closed and still know the animal's state from gait and breath alone after ten minutes, the readout is dead and so is the game. Three days.
biggest_risks: Legibility: an inscrutable utility AI reads as randomness and unfairness. The mind must be predictable enough to master while never feeling like a puppet — a narrow band. The credibility mechanic risks collapsing into 'just another cooldown' if the player never experiences the true-emergency-ignored moment; that moment must be engineered to happen in the first hour. Procedural quadruped locomotion carries the entire visual case for the game and is the hardest single piece of code here; if the animal does not look alive, nothing works.
feasibility_notes: Ideal for the stack, because everything expensive is simulation rather than art. One creature archetype: ~18-bone 2D skeleton, spring-damper muscles, two-bone IK legs, a CPG gait driver whose frequency, duty factor, stride length and asymmetry are read straight off heart rate, fatigue, heat and tendon strain — one animal at 60fps is nothing. Terrain as layered heightfield with parallax, heat shimmer as a screen-space refraction shader, dust and sweat as instanced particles. Audio is the real weapon and it is cheap: breath synthesised as filtered noise with a two-phase envelope driven by actual respiration rate, heartbeat as a modulated sine thump on true HR and stroke volume, hoof impacts triggered by real foot-contact events, wind from the sim. The player learns to hear the animal's state before they can see it — roughly 200 lines of WebAudio.

name: SLOW MATCH
pitch: You are the firekeeper of a valley that needs to burn. Not a firefighter — a farmer of fire. You choose where and, far more importantly, *at what hour* to put flame into a landscape, and then you live with what the wind, the slope and the dew decide to do with it. The fire will not obey you; it will only respond, four hours late, to conditions you set before you knew what the afternoon would bring.
central_verb: Commit — to choose the hour. Lighting is one click; the game is which minute of which day you spend it in, with a forecast you cannot trust.
player_role: The player is a steward with no cancel button. Onscreen is an oblique-top-down valley as a continuous field (fuel load, moisture, heat, char) rather than tiles, with a wind field shaped by slope, aspect and the diurnal cycle: overnight cold air pools and the fire lies down and creeps; by 13:00 the upslope wind runs and the fire stands up. Verbs: drop a light; order one of two ground crews to rake a fuel break (they walk at human speed and will abandon the line if fire comes within their refusal radius); wet a short black line; sample moisture by touch; and wait at 1x/4x/16x. There is no extinguish verb.
loop_10s: Watch the plume lean. Its tilt tells you the wind before the anemometer does. The backing fire is creeping downhill exactly as intended, but the smoke it makes has just covered the creek and you have lost the visual — you flip to the IR overlay, which is a coarse thermal grid refreshed every thirty seconds, and now you are steering a fire you can only see in the past tense.
loop_2min: The afternoon decision. The forecast cone says the wind swings north at 14:00 with 60% confidence. Light the north face now and you get the four hours of burning you need for the year — but if the swing comes early, fire crosses the saddle into the old grove, which needs low fire to open its cones and dies outright to crown fire. Wait for certainty and the fuel dries past your window and you lose the whole season. Meanwhile your two crews are the only labour you have: rake a line you probably will not need, or send them to sample the moisture in the gully you definitely want to know about.
mastery_loop: Reading slope, aspect, hour, fuel continuity and dew point as a single object. Discovering the real techniques: backing a fire downhill against the wind all night while you sleep so it takes exactly the fuel you wanted; lighting two fires so their convection columns draw together and consume the ground between them in a controlled indraft; knowing that the gully will lie down at dusk and therefore that the risky light is safe if it is late enough; and, hardest of all, learning when to let a patch go.
tension: Three tugs at once. The fire you need is the fire that is barely survivable. The safe fire — a smoky, low-intensity backing burn — is the one that blinds you, while the fire you can see clearly is the one that is getting away. And the window versus certainty problem: information improves as the hour approaches, and the fuel gets worse.
failure: Escape: the burn takes the village at the valley mouth or the old grove, and you do not lose — you keep playing in a valley that is permanently different, which is worse. Campaign failure comes in two flavours at the end of the decade: a choked valley, where fuel is so continuous that any ignition anywhere becomes unstoppable and you have lost the ability to act at all; or a scoured one, where you burned so often that the wet gully species is gone and the mosaic is a monotone. The score is not points. It is the burn-history map.
expression: After a decade the valley is a painting of your decisions — a mosaic of patch ages you can read at a glance. Another player can look at your valley and tell whether you were an aggressive early-season burner working in daylight with big margins, or a patient night-burner who took small bites against the wind for ten years and never once needed a crew.
novice_vs_expert: Novice lights downwind at midday because that is when they can see, watches it run, then panics and rakes lines in front of a fire that is already faster than a walking human. Expert lights the top of the slope at dusk and goes to sleep. Novice treats smoke as an annoyance; expert budgets blindness in advance and positions crews where they will not need to be seen.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: Because the valley remembers. Every year's mosaic redefines next year's problem — last year's burn is this year's break, and the seven-year unburned gully is a constraint that gets more expensive every season you honour it. And because the emergent techniques are genuinely discoverable over hours: the indraft double-light is not in any tutorial and lands like learning a real craft.
why_not_an_existing_genre: It is not a disaster or firefighting game — fire is the goal, not the enemy, and there is no extinguish verb. It is not a citybuilder or management sim — nothing is built, there is no economy, no growth curve, no unlocks. It is not an RTS — there are two crews, they walk, and they refuse. The source of decisions is prediction and irreversible pre-commitment into a continuous nonlinear system whose response arrives hours later and cannot be cancelled; the mastery is meteorological and physical intuition, not optimisation.
falsifying_prototype: A 256x256 fuel/moisture field, a wind field with slope acceleration and a diurnal cycle, one ignition verb, one rake verb, one goal: burn 60% of the north face without letting fire cross the creek. Kill criterion: if players cannot build a working intuition within three attempts — if attempt four does not feel qualitatively smarter than attempt one — the sim is a chaos toy and there is no game in it. Secondary test: does smoke occlusion read as tension or as a camera bug? Four days.
biggest_risks: The fire model is the entire game and its tuning band is narrow: too chaotic reads as unfair, too tame reads as a colouring book. Real-time-only means a bad commit costs fifteen minutes, so escapes must be interesting rather than terminal. Smoke blindness may simply annoy. And cultural burning is a living Indigenous practice — either treat it with real respect and research, or build a clearly fictional frame; a careless middle would be the worst outcome.
feasibility_notes: Almost entirely GPU field work, which is the sweet spot here. Ping-pong float textures at 512x512: one pass for combustion/fuel/moisture, one for wind advection with slope and thermal columns, one for smoke density advection, one composite pass with emissive tone mapping, heat refraction and smoke occlusion drawn from the same density field the sim uses. Comfortably 60fps with room to spare. Terrain, fuel type and moisture generated procedurally per valley in Python or in-browser noise. Audio is synthesised directly from sim state and is the best cheap effect in the whole design: crackle as a filtered impulse train whose rate follows the ignition-event count, roar as filtered noise with cutoff and gain tracking total heat release, and a low sub rumble when convection couples with the wind — so the player *hears* the fire stand up several seconds before the plume shows it.

name: COINAGE
pitch: You keep a lamp above a coastal settlement that cannot hear you. You can flash thirty-six distinguishable signs and nothing more — and none of them mean anything until history puts a meaning next to them. The villagers build the dictionary, not you; they learn by coincidence, they gossip, and meanings drift. You can see the storm four hours before they can, and you must have spent the calm season inventing a word for it.
central_verb: Coin — to give a sign a meaning by placing it next to an event, and thereafter to spend, defend, or abandon that meaning.
player_role: The player is an oracle with no language. Onscreen: a night coast in 2.5D silhouette — a tower, a settlement of warm window-lights, small moving lanterns, ships out on black water, weather as fields. Signs are composed from three axes (colour x rhythm x duration, ~36-48 combinations); you may emit roughly two per night, limited by oil. About 120 inhabitants across four factions each maintain an association table from perceived signs to event categories (storm, fish-run, sickness, raiders, frost, nothing), strengthened by co-occurrence weighted by salience and recency, and spread — mutating and simplifying as it goes — by gossip. Crucially each faction attends to a different axis: fishers to colour, the temple to rhythm, children to duration. An unseen sign inherits meaning from known signs by similarity *in the dimensions that listener attends to*, so you can coin new words with controlled connotation, and say two different things to two audiences with one lamp.
loop_10s: A squall line is visible from the tower; the fishers are still on the water. Open the meaning map: the blot for amber-double-brief is 70% storm among fishers, saturated, but among the temple it is a wash of pale nothing. Flash it. Watch lantern dots turn on the quay and start moving — or not.
loop_2min: Autumn. You know frost is coming and you have no sign for cold. Options: spend clean, unused white-stutter-held on it now, burning a fresh word on a single event; or extend amber-stutter, which you deliberately coined last spring on the harmless, salient, perfectly predictable arrival of the first mackerel, and which the fishers therefore read as 'the season turns, move' — they will half-understand, and the temple will read nothing at all, which may be exactly what you want, because the temple has begun preaching your lamp in advance and is becoming a rival author of your language.
mastery_loop: Learning the associative model well enough to farm it: manufacturing correlations in quiet seasons by putting a fresh sign next to a cheap, certain, salient event; building a compositional morphology so that new words are guessable rather than empty; aiming a sign along one faction's attention axis so it is legible to them and invisible to another; using the temple's prophecy as a free amplifier; and deliberately sacrificing one sign as a decoy so the drift lands on it instead of on a word you need.
tension: Vocabulary is capital and crises are demand, and the only way to mint a word is to let an event happen next to it. So every meaning you own was paid for by something that already happened, and the emergency you can see coming is exactly the one you have no word for. Underneath that: silence is not free — a dark lamp on the night of a wreck becomes a sign too, one you did not choose.
failure: Semantic collapse: associations flatten, the lamp becomes noise, and no signal changes any behaviour. You are still in the tower, you can still see the storm coming four hours out, and you have no way to be heard. Or doctrinal capture: a faction fixes a meaning that gets people killed and enforces it against evidence, so your correct warnings now reliably cause the wrong action — the bell that means 'gather in the hall' during a fire. You lose language, not health.
expression: The dictionary is the artifact. One player ends the decade with eight precise, compositional, well-defended words; another with three enormous overloaded signs that function like cult sacraments and are obeyed with terrifying speed and appalling precision. Both are legible to another player, who can read your entire ethics off your language in a minute.
novice_vs_expert: The novice invents a signal in the emergency, flashes it desperately, and nothing happens — because a sign with no history is not a warning, it is a light. The expert spent the calm spring attaching amber-stutter to the first mackerel, so that in autumn amber-stutter-held is understood by the fishers as movement toward the water and by the temple as nothing at all. The novice fights drift by shouting; the expert lets a doomed word drift and quietly builds its replacement two coordinates away.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: Because founding a language and maintaining one are different games, and the second is harder. Hour two is repair work: a word has inverted through two coincidences, the temple is preaching ahead of you, and the young fishers learned their vocabulary from gossip rather than from the lamp. You are no longer inventing meaning, you are defending it against a culture that has started producing its own — which is precisely the moment the ward stops obeying.
why_not_an_existing_genre: It is not a god game: no miracles, no direct effect on the world, no terrain to lift. It is not a management sim: the only resource is oil, and there is no economy, growth or unlock. It is not a narrative or dialogue game: there is no dialogue tree, no writing, no words at all. The decisions are about *establishing reference* under scarcity, against a population that authors meaning independently of you. I know of no game whose mastery is the management of a semantic drift you started.
falsifying_prototype: Forty villagers, one faction, twelve signs, four event types, three in-game years, with the raw association matrix visible. Kill criterion: if the player does not, unprompted, discover that words must be coined *before* they are needed — if the pre-investment insight has to be told to them — the loop's core lesson is not emergent and the design fails. Second criterion: the meaning map must be readable at a glance; if players have to inspect numbers to know what a sign currently means, the whole thing is a black box. Four to five days.
biggest_risks: Legibility is the whole risk: associative learning is fog unless the readout is exceptional, and the meaning map has to do work that no existing game UI has ever had to do. Second, the player may feel merely powerless rather than responsible — crises must be genuinely winnable with a good vocabulary, so that failure reads as 'I did not build the word' and never as 'they were always going to drown'. Third, too little coincidence and it degenerates into a solvable optimisation puzzle; too much and it is noise. Fourth, the subject matter — manipulating a population's beliefs — must be handled with enough weight that it does not read as a cynical toy.
feasibility_notes: The simulation is trivially cheap: 120 agents x 48 signs x 6 meanings is ~35k floats updated once per in-game night, plus a gossip pass. All the budget goes into presentation, which is exactly what this stack is good at: procedural night coast, a volumetric lamp beam as a screen-space cone with god-ray accumulation, sea and rain as shaders, warm window lights with bloom, lantern dots as instanced sprites with pathing. The meaning map is a custom fragment shader — signs as blots in a 2D projection of sign-space, colour mixture showing the meaning distribution, saturation showing conviction, fringing showing inter-faction disagreement — and it will be the most striking image in the game. Audio: bells and lamp tones by modal synthesis (a handful of damped resonators, ~40 lines of WebAudio, sounds genuinely beautiful), surf from filtered noise with breaking envelopes, and a granular crowd murmur whose density tracks how many people are awake and moving. Zero authored art assets anywhere.

name: RESIDUAL
pitch: You are handed the frozen aftermath of a physical failure — a collapsed silo of grain, a cracked kiln, a pipe run that burst — and no record of what happened. You have a simulator of the same physics, a handful of dials for the initial conditions, and a strict budget of runs. You guess a past, run it forward, and the game shows you the difference between your world and the real one as a shimmering residual field; the whole art is learning to read the shape of your own wrongness.
central_verb: Reconstruct — propose a past, run it forward, and read the error.
player_role: A failure examiner who cannot observe the event, only its corpse and their own counterfactuals. The player perceives a settled cross-section (cold, still, ~256x256 grid of material/heat/stress), manipulates a hypothesis rack (a draggable origin marker, three continuous sliders such as initial moisture 0-1, load mass, fill angle, plus two discrete switches such as valve open/closed), and produces one thing: a filed verdict with a stated confidence. They never gain power over the scene; they gain, or fail to gain, the right to be sure.
loop_10s: Nudge the origin marker four pixels down the slope, press SPACE, watch ~900 sim steps play out in 2.5s, press TAB to flip on the residual overlay: the crescent of blue (too much material) on the lee side has flipped to orange (too little). You overshot. One run of your nine is gone.
loop_2min: Form a hypothesis — 'the wall went first, then the fill' — and find it explains the entire west face to within noise but leaves a stubborn ring of residual at the door. Rings mean timing, not geometry, so you stop touching the slider you were about to touch, spend a third of an assay on a region-only residual at the door, and confirm the ring is not going away for any timing you can afford to test. Which means the answer is not in the debris at all: you must buy the witness (a soot-chemistry sample, 2 runs) to separate the two pasts that both fit.
mastery_loop: Learning the residual's visual grammar and, above all, learning the residual floor. The truth run always contains a little physics your simulator does not expose (a draft, a hairline flaw), so a perfect match is impossible; speckled, uncorrelated residual means you have hit chaos and every further dial-turn is wasted budget. Experts recognise irreducible residual in one glance and immediately switch from tuning to buying a different observable. Deeper mastery is diagnosticity: knowing which 15% of the wreckage carries information about initial conditions and which 85% looks the same under every hypothesis, so you never pay to look at it.
tension: Runs are the only way to learn and the only thing you can spend, and confidence is scored: filing right at 95% is worth a lot, filing wrong at 95% is ruinous, filing right at 60% is worth little. So every run is a bet that the information it returns will move you up a confidence band. The agonising moment is holding two surviving hypotheses that produce indistinguishable visible residual, with three runs left and a carried reserve you keep for future cases: spend them trying to separate two pasts that may be genuinely inseparable, or file at 60% now and bank the rest.
failure: Filing a confident wrong verdict. There is no death and no health. The consequence is causal and delayed: your verdict becomes the recommended fix, and in a later case that fix is a component in the scene — so case 9 is harder specifically because you must now diagnose a failure you caused, without being told that is what you are doing. Refusing to file at all forfeits the case and the banked reserve, so paralysis is also a loss condition.
expression: Budget style is legible and personal. Some players are run-heavy brute-forcers who sweep parameter space; others buy the discriminating witness first and only then touch a dial; others file fast at 80% across the board and get rich on reserve. The pinned-snapshot notebook — the residuals a player chose to keep and annotate — is a visible record of how they think, and two players' notebooks on the same case show two different investigations.
novice_vs_expert: A novice tunes every slider toward zero residual everywhere, treats all error as reducible, and burns nine runs shaving noise off a wall that would look identical under every hypothesis. An expert glances at the settled scene, identifies the two features that are actually hypothesis-sensitive, spends run one on a deliberately extreme guess to see which direction the residual moves, and files at 95% on run four with five in the bank. The expert's defining skill is a list of things they did not bother to look at.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The residual grammar is a real learned language with more vocabulary than an hour can exhaust, and it is generated rather than authored, so it keeps paying off across new physical domains (granular, thermal, fracture, fluid) where the same shapes mean analogous things. The confidence economy means a skilled player is not playing the same game as a beginner — they are playing a bolder one, with a reserve that lets them attack cases nobody could afford to attack fresh. And the campaign's causal debt means the back half of the run is populated by your own past errors, content generated by the player rather than the designer.
why_not_an_existing_genre: Deduction games present a fixed authored evidence set over a discrete solution space; you search a room. Here the evidence does not exist until you manufacture it — every counterfactual run is an experiment you paid for, the solution space is continuous and partly non-identifiable, and the core skill is estimating in advance which measurement would actually discriminate. That is inverse inference under a measurement budget, and no genre currently does it. It is also not a physics sandbox: the simulation is not the toy, the difference between two simulations is.
falsifying_prototype: One physical system only: granular collapse of a stack against a wall, 256x256 GPU sim, five hidden parameters (three continuous, two discrete), one unmodelled perturbation the player cannot access. Run/compare loop, signed residual overlay, hard budget of eight runs, one binary verdict with three confidence bands. Ship it to six people for twenty minutes each. It is dead if they cannot articulate a rule of the form 'crescent means angle, ring means timing' by the end, or if they say 'I just kept nudging until the colour went away' — that means the residual carries no readable grammar and the game is blind gradient descent.
biggest_risks: (1) The residual may never develop a legible grammar — if error shapes are not consistently caused by particular parameter errors, the game degenerates into manual hill-climbing. This is a sim-design problem, not a UI problem, and must be validated first. (2) Chaos calibration: too sensitive and nothing is learnable, too stable and one run solves everything. (3) The confidence scoring must feel fair, not punitive — after filing, players must be able to see exactly which observable they should have bought. (4) A frozen still-life is hard to make beautiful; the sim playback and the residual bloom carry all of the game's motion.
feasibility_notes: Ideal for the stack. The sim is a fragment-shader ping-pong over two or three RGBA32F textures at 256x256; several hundred steps run in a fraction of a second, so full playback is cheap and scrubbing is free. Determinism is guaranteed by construction: the truth final state is produced at case-load time by running the identical shader with hidden parameters, never loaded as an image, so the player's simulator and reality are bit-identical apart from the deliberate unmodelled term. Residual is a one-pass diff shader into a diverging colour ramp (LUT baked in Python/PIL). No art assets — the scene is material fields rendered with a lighting shader. Audio is procedural: playback drives granular noise and settling ticks, and the residual overlay has a tone whose beating rate tracks total error, so convergence can be heard with eyes on the geometry.

name: STILL CULTURE
pitch: A living medium grows in a dish under your hands, and every instrument that would tell you what it is doing also damages it. You steer it toward a target morphology with coarse, blind actuators — heat, nutrient, shade, shear — while the only cheap information is the way it moves and the sound it makes. Expertise is the slow replacement of measurement with recognition, until you can shape a culture almost without looking at it.
central_verb: Withhold — decide, second by second, not to look.
player_role: A steward of something with its own agenda, which you can influence but not command and cannot directly perceive. On screen is a full-bleed dark-field render of a reaction-diffusion field plus ~4000 motile particles, breathing and branching in real time, with a faint target stencil and a clock. The player becomes the thing that must act on an unreliable reading of a system, and is scored both on what the culture becomes and on how much of it they burned finding out.
loop_10s: The lobe at four o'clock is thickening. You hold RMB and scroll the thermal ring out to 60% radius, hear the hum drop a third, release. The medium's motion field goes briefly coherent — good sign — then starts to shimmer at the edge, which is either the start of a branch or the start of a collapse, and those want opposite interventions. Your hand hovers over the fluorescence key.
loop_2min: You commit to not probing, run a nutrient drip at the base of the lobe, and wait forty seconds for the hum to resolve — the two outcomes have different beat frequencies once they are far enough along. It resolves the wrong way: it was the ropy variant, and it has locked. You have eight minutes, three fluorescence charges, and a stencil that no longer matches anything in the dish, so you stop steering toward the stencil and start steering toward the nearest morphology you can still reach — which means deliberately shearing the healthy half of the dish to free the mass.
mastery_loop: Building a private library of free cues that substitute for expensive ones. The hum (synthesised live from field statistics: dominant spatial frequency to pitch, variance to noise floor, bifurcation to audible beating), the meniscus behaviour at the dish edge, the way particle motion goes coherent a few seconds before a structural commitment. None is decisive alone; the expert's skill is a joint reading of three ambiguous free channels that beats one decisive expensive one. Above that sits the real mastery: knowing that most of the culture self-corrects, and only two or three moments per session are worth a probe at all.
tension: Fluorescence reveals species concentration in a disc and bleaches it, costing that region ~90 seconds of growth you do not have. Aspirate returns exact numbers for four hidden variables and permanently removes mass, punching a hole the medium must heal around. Acoustic sweep is cheap and whole-dish but aggregate — it says something is bifurcating, never where. Meanwhile each culture carries two or three latent binaries (is this seed the ropy variant?) that invert the correct response and that free channels genuinely cannot separate until it is nearly too late. Blind play cannot win the hard strains; instrument-heavy play cannot pass viability. The agony always has the same shape: probe now and lose the thing you were trying to save, or wait and find out for free but possibly too late.
failure: Two distinct losses, both epistemic. The culture dies or misses the morphology because you waited for certainty that never arrived. Or it matches the stencil in a scarred, non-viable state — you got the shape by interrogating it to death, and the assay rejects it. Scar load is visible throughout as a dulling in the dark-field render and a roughness in the hum, so the player watches the price of their own curiosity accumulating in real time.
expression: Cultures are artefacts. A finished dish is a specific object with your intervention history written into it — bleached discs, aspirate craters, the asymmetry of the lobes — and exports as a seed string others can grow. Playstyle divides sharply into blind farmers who work almost entirely by ear and instrument-first players who buy certainty early and then execute; both can win, and their dishes look nothing alike.
novice_vs_expert: A novice probes reactively — something looks odd, so they fluoresce it — and ends with a dish that matches the stencil at 80% and fails viability, having spent all eight charges on questions whose answers changed no action they took. An expert probes once, early, at the single place where the latent binary branches their plan, then plays the remaining fifteen minutes on the hum and the motion field alone, taking two large coarse actions instead of twenty small ones. Asked why they ignored the collapsing north edge, the expert says the medium fixes that itself.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The strain lineage. You keep a sample from your best culture and it seeds the next session with drifted constants drawn from the same family, so the shape of the dynamics transfers while exact thresholds betray you — intuition compounds without becoming rote, and the re-learning cost is small enough to be pleasurable. Scars are inherited too: a lineage you interrogated heavily becomes a lineage that responds badly to interrogation, so knowledge debt accrues across sessions and forces a real long-arc choice between a strain you understand and a clean one you do not.
why_not_an_existing_genre: Cellular-automata and reaction-diffusion pieces are toys: no goal, no failure, no cost to looking. Colony and management sims give you full information and make scarcity material. Here the scarce thing is state knowledge and its price is paid in the substrate itself, so the central decision — do I look — has no analogue in a management game where observation is free and unlimited. Nor is it fog of war: fog lifts when you move into it, whereas here every act of seeing permanently damages the thing you are trying to preserve, and the win condition explicitly scores restraint.
falsifying_prototype: One strain family, one target morphology, a ten-minute clock. Gray-Scott plus advection at 512x512, the live hum synth, three actuators (thermal ring, nutrient drip, shear) and one probe (fluorescence, six charges), plus one latent binary that inverts the correct thermal response. Two scores at the end: shape match and scar load. It is dead if testers report the ten minutes felt like waiting, or if a policy of never probing scores as well as a considered one — the first means the free channels are not tense enough, the second means the latent state is not doing its job.
biggest_risks: (1) It could feel like watching paint dry — the free ambient channels must be moment-to-moment gripping and genuinely informative, or the 'do I look' decision has no stakes. (2) Degenerate optimum: if never probing wins, the game collapses; the latent binaries must be lethal, common, and truly unreadable from ambient cues. (3) Readability of a continuous field — morphology match must be intuitively judgeable by eye, not a hidden score the player cannot predict. (4) Strain drift tuning is delicate: too much and mastery never accumulates, too little and it becomes memorisation. (5) The audio channel is load-bearing rather than decorative, so a player on laptop speakers or with sound off must still have a viable, weaker read.
feasibility_notes: The strongest fit of the three. Gray-Scott plus an advected particle layer is a handful of fragment shaders over ping-pong RGBA32F FBOs; 512x512 with 4000 particles is comfortably 60fps on the target GPU with headroom for a rich render pass (dark-field lighting, thin-film iridescence, depth of field). Zero art assets — the visual identity is entirely the simulation. Audio is a genuine mechanic and fully procedural: downsample the field to 16x16 once per frame, read it back on the CPU (cheap enough to tolerate the stall at that size; one frame of latency is harmless) and drive an additive/granular WebAudio voice bank from the statistics. Python/PIL bakes colour LUTs and target stencils offline. No physics library, no build step, no npm.

name: HEARSAY
pitch: A band of two hundred creatures crosses a landscape by acting on what they believe, and they are wrong about several things that will kill them. You can see the poison flat and the freeze line; you have no voice. All you can do is leave evidence — a scent, a warmed stone, a bent reed, a killed plant — and every lie you tell costs you the future credibility of the channel you told it through.
central_verb: Convince — translate what you know into another mind's belief through a lossy, exhaustible channel.
player_role: A wordless presence responsible for something that does not obey you and cannot be told anything. You perceive a wide procedural landscape under a moving sun, ~250 motes of light moving as a colony with visible hesitation and fan-out, and an overlay of your own knowledge that is itself partial and a day stale (the freeze line is a probability band, not a line). You never see their beliefs; you infer them from how their scouts spread and how tightly the colony murmur harmonises.
loop_10s: The scout fan opens toward the salt flat instead of the ridge — they have smelled the mirage water, a true signal pointing at a lethal place. You drift to the ridge and kill a stand of grass there, an honest negative about water that therefore costs no credibility, but also does not say 'come here'. The fan narrows by ten degrees. Not enough.
loop_2min: You spend your last strong scent laying a line north and they follow — buying you the flat, costing you the crossing, because the scent channel is now the only one they still trust and it is empty. Halfway north a scout finds nothing, that channel's credence drops, and the colony mills in dissonance. You are down to the presence channel, which is cheap and works, and every use raises their credence in you while lowering their credence in their own scouting. You use it once and promise yourself not again.
mastery_loop: Credibility economics with hidden belief inference. Every channel (scent, ground-warmth, tracks, cairns, plant-death, your own presence) carries a per-colony credence that rises slowly on confirmation and collapses on disconfirmation — but disconfirmation only happens if they actually go and check, so untested lies are free, and lies they act on and survive can even come out ahead on mixed evidence. Expert play is banking credibility during easy stretches by leading them to real but inconvenient resources, spending it only on beliefs that are both lethal and self-reinforcing, and reading the belief field off scout-fan geometry rather than buying the expensive read (sit inside the murmur for thirty seconds, immobile, all breath spent, for a blurred render of what they think).
tension: The environment is an honest, competing information source that sometimes tells them true things leading somewhere fatal, and true evidence is very hard to argue against. Your own overlay is stale, so you are committing scarce credibility to a freeze line that is only a probability band. And the cheapest, most reliable channel — lingering where they can see you — is the one that destroys them: a colony whose credence in your presence outgrows its credence in its own scouting has stopped learning the world.
failure: The colony starves, freezes, or is eaten. Or the subtler and more memorable loss: the leash. They survive the season, but presence-credence exceeds every other channel, and the run ends at dawn with two hundred motes sitting still, waiting for you instead of foraging. A third failure is reputational — colonies exchange beliefs and channel credences when they meet, so a band you burned in week two can teach a band you have never touched to disbelieve scent, and you arrive at a late-season colony already bankrupt in the channel you needed.
expression: Your season leaves a legible signature: which channels each region's colonies now trust, and how much. Two players who both got their band to the wintering ground will have done it with completely different instruments — one who never lied and spent the season broke but trusted, one who ran scent to zero early and improvised on tracks and cairns for the rest. The end-of-run screen is not a score but a map of what the world's colonies believe, authored entirely by the player's conduct.
novice_vs_expert: A novice treats every false belief as a problem to fix, corrects the colony's drift toward a barren valley on day three, and reaches the crossing with no credibility anywhere and a band half-taught to follow them. An expert watches the same drift, recognises the colony's own scouting will correct it in a day and a half at the cost of one thin meal, says nothing, and still holds two strong scents and an intact reputation when the freeze band tightens. Their defining skill is silence.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The opponent is a belief system rather than a difficulty curve, so it keeps generating situations no designer wrote: honest signals that happen to point at death, lies accidentally confirmed, a colony that ends up right for the wrong reason and therefore trusts the wrong channel forever. Credibility persists across colonies and across the season, so an hour in you are playing a long reputational game with real inherited state, and the ceiling skill — reading a belief field off flocking geometry — is perceptual and keeps sharpening. Later seasons introduce colonies that have already met you.
why_not_an_existing_genre: It is not a god game or indirect-control puzzler: those give you terrain edits and physical shoves, and the creatures are pathfinders reacting to world state. Here the agents are inference engines, world state barely touches their behaviour directly, and your entire interface is the evidence stream feeding their model. Nor is it stealth or social deduction — you are not hiding a fact, you are manufacturing beliefs in a system that keeps a running audit of your reliability, and the resource you spend is the future usability of a communication channel. The decision 'is this wrong belief worth correcting?' exists in no current genre.
falsifying_prototype: One colony of 200 agents, one 96x96 belief grid, one procedural valley with a single hidden lethal feature (a poison seep that smells like water) and a single deadline (a freeze band advancing from the north). Four channels with credence tracking, the murmur synth, no other colonies. Fifteen-minute run. It is dead if testers spam the strongest channel every time and win, if they cannot tell from the scout fan whether the colony believes them, or if they report they were solving a pathing problem rather than arguing with someone. That last one is the real test: it must feel like persuasion, not routing.
biggest_risks: (1) Legibility of the hidden belief field — if the player cannot read intent off flocking behaviour the game is opaque, and the obvious fix (just show the belief field) destroys the concept. Everything depends on tuning fan-out, hesitation and murmur dissonance into a readable behavioural language. (2) The colony's inference model must be simple enough to be intuited but rich enough to surprise. (3) Anthropomorphism doing the work — the concept could coast on 'aww, little creatures' instead of delivering real decisions. (4) The leash failure is the best idea here and the easiest to make feel like arbitrary punishment; it must be visibly accruing long before it triggers. (5) Feedback latency — consequences arrive minutes after the act, which risks the player never connecting cause to effect; an end-of-day 'what changed and why' recap may be necessary.
feasibility_notes: Comfortable. 250-800 agents with flocking plus a scouting state machine runs on the CPU in a few milliseconds; the belief grid is a 96x96 float array with a cheap diffusion-and-decay update, well under budget. Terrain is SDF/noise in a fragment shader with a moving sun and cheap atmospheric scattering — 2.5D, no meshes, no textures, no animation library; agents are point sprites with motion trails, exactly the 'beauty from motion and light' the stack is good at. Evidence acts are particle emitters plus a scalar written into a scent field. Audio is a real mechanic and pure WebAudio: ~24 detuned voices whose collective pitch spread is driven by belief variance, so consensus is an audible chord and disagreement audible beating. Python/PIL bakes terrain colour ramps and the sun LUT. No build step, no dependencies, no authored assets.

name: Objective
pitch: A gather of molten glass on the end of a rod, seen in cross-section, glowing by its own temperature. You never sculpt it — you set rotation, torch position and breath, and the glass sags, swells and stiffens according to its own viscosity, three to six seconds behind your hands. When it is finally cold you shine light through the geometry you actually made and find out what you made. You are building one telescope objective out of a series of elements, and every flaw you accept becomes a hard constraint on the next piece.
central_verb: Lead — as in leading a moving target. Every input acts on a body that is several seconds in the future, so the play verb is not 'shape' but 'apply a tendency and stop before the result arrives'.
player_role: A glasswright making optical elements for an instrument that does not exist yet. You perceive: an axisymmetric profile glowing blackbody red-to-white straight off its temperature field; wall thickness legible only where the glass is thin enough to see through; sag accelerating as the neck passes its softening point; and an internal stress field that is completely invisible unless you spend one of your three polariscope glances per piece. Controls: mouse X = torch position along the piece, mouse Y = torch standoff (heat rate vs. depth of penetration), wheel = rod rotation 0-180 rpm, hold Space = breath (a real lung model: pressure builds over ~0.8 s and decays after release, so you cannot pulse it precisely), Shift+drag = press a wet paddle or jacks against the profile at a point, which does nothing unless the local viscosity is inside a narrow window, keys 1-4 = jacks / paddle / shears / tweezers. There is no shape editor, no undo, and no direct control of any coordinate.
loop_10s: The tip reads 1120 C, the neck 830 C. You want the belly to swell without the neck necking down under its own weight. So you wind rotation up to 120 rpm to spin the sag out, put the torch 40% along the piece at close standoff, and then wait — heat needs about 2.5 s to reach the core at that wall thickness. You blow before the surface looks ready, because by the time the surface looks ready the core is already too soft, and you release breath a beat before the bulge reaches the size you want. Then you pull the torch and watch it arrive.
loop_2min: One element, cradle to annealer: gather, mark the shoulder, open the bubble, work the front curve, flatten the back, transfer to the punty, shear off, and get it into the annealer above 520 C before the outside outruns the inside. Then the cold test — the game ray-traces your actual profile with three wavelengths and shows you the spot diagram, the focal length, and the smear your residual stress adds. That readout is the only judge, and it arrives ninety seconds after the decisions that caused it.
mastery_loop: Learning the material's transfer function. That surface colour lies about core temperature, and by exactly how much at each wall thickness. That rotation both fights sag and thins the wall, so speed is never free. That every time a thick section crosses 520 C with a gradient across it you bank permanent stress you will not see until the annealer. That the fastest route to a given curve is often to heat somewhere you do not want to change and let gravity do the work while you rotate. Expertise is a felt model of thermal lag, and it is trained by the piece cracking, not by a tutorial.
tension: Heat is the only thing that lets you work the glass and the only thing that ruins it. Every second in the flame is simultaneously progress and damage, and the damage is invisible. Compounding that: a piece looks finished and perfect while still hot, and the decision to spend forty more seconds relieving stress you cannot observe will visibly deform the surface you just spent ninety seconds getting right.
failure: Two kinds, both delayed. The piece pings in the annealer forty seconds after you set it down and a fracture line walks across your best surface. Or it survives, goes cold, and the ray trace reports a focal length 6% long with strong spherical aberration — a perfectly sound object that is the wrong object. Cold glass cannot be reworked without a full reheat cycle that destroys the surface figure. The instrument only holds so many elements, and each scrap costs you a batch of glass.
expression: The compensation chain is authored by your own hands. Element four must be designed around the errors in one through three, so two players building the same instrument end up with visibly different glass: one runs hot and fast and produces thin, light, stress-heavy elements and a short fast train; another runs cool and thick, fights sag constantly, and ends with a long heavy instrument that is optically forgiving. There is also a signature in how you use the polariscope glances — some players spend all three on the first element and then work blind on faith.
novice_vs_expert: A novice acts on what the glass looks like now, so they always overshoot, then chase the overshoot with a correction that also overshoots, and the piece dies of accumulated thermal cycles rather than any single mistake. An expert acts on where the glass will be in four seconds, pulls the torch early, uses rotation instead of breath wherever possible, and spends most of the session doing nothing while heat travels. The clearest tell: a novice's torch is always on; an expert's torch is on maybe a third of the time.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: Because the instrument accumulates and the constraint space narrows from your own errors, not from a difficulty curve. By element five you are no longer trying to hit a spec — you are trying to hit the one remaining spec that would rescue the four pieces already in the tube. The craft problem gets harder and more particular the longer you play, and it gets harder in a shape unique to your session.
why_not_an_existing_genre: There is no object placement, no shape editing, no undo, no inventory and no score. The only inputs are rates applied to a body with thermal inertia, and the only judgement is a physical ray trace through the geometry you produced. Existing crafting systems resolve a recipe into an item; here there is no recipe and no item — there is a continuous body whose state is the integral of everything you did to it. The nearest relatives are surgery and flight sims, and neither of those has the material itself as the antagonist.
falsifying_prototype: A 192-ring axisymmetric profile with temperature diffusion, viscosity(T), gravity, surface tension and internal pressure; one torch, one blow key, rotation; no tools, no scoring; plus the cold ray trace. Two tests. First: can experienced testers, within fifteen minutes, reliably put a bulge where they intended and stop it there? If anticipation is not learnable in fifteen minutes it will never be learnable. Second: after seeing the cold optical result, can a tester articulate which hot action caused it? If not, the test reads as a slot machine and the whole loop is dead regardless of how good the sim looks.
biggest_risks: The viscous window may be untunable — either mushy, where nothing the player does is precise, or twitchy, where nothing is forgiving; that band could be genuinely thin. Axisymmetry caps expressivity: no off-axis work, no asymmetric pieces, which may make the space of interesting shapes too small to sustain an hour. And the cold test needs a legible causal readout (wall-thickness profile overlaid on the aberration curve, stress map revealed post-mortem) or players will never build the mental model that makes the delayed judgement fair.
feasibility_notes: Ideal for the stack. 192 rings integrated at 240 Hz with sub-stepping is nothing. Rendering: revolve the profile into a strip mesh, screen-space refraction with three-wavelength dispersion, and emission taken directly from a Planck fit to the temperature field — the glow is literally the simulation, so the game's beauty needs zero authored art. Annealing cracks render as procedural fracture polylines. Audio is entirely WebAudio: filtered noise for the torch with roar intensity following gas flow, a resonant tube for the blowpipe whose pitch tracks the enclosed bubble volume, and a small modal bank for the crack ping. Python/PIL only needed for a couple of noise LUTs. No assets, no streaming, comfortably 60fps.

name: Perfusion
pitch: A living vascular mat spread across a backlit pane, carrying flow from three intakes to demands that change without warning. It thickens whatever it uses and kills whatever it does not — including every alternate route you would need in an emergency. You have a scalpel, a clamp, a graft needle and a nutrient dropper. Your job is not to build the network. Your job is to stop it from optimising itself to death.
central_verb: Restrict — the primary action is deliberately making the system worse right now so that it still has options in ninety seconds.
player_role: A keeper responsible for something that keeps making irreversible investments without consulting you.
