You perceive vessel radius as line thickness, flow rate as the speed and brightness of travelling pulses, pressure as hue (cool blue low, amber high), and conviction as phase: a vessel that has carried steady flow for thirty seconds pulses in lock with its neighbours, while an undecided one visibly jitters and will atrophy. Demand is never shown — you read it from how hard a sink pulls, as a pressure gradient. Controls: left-drag along a vessel is a scalpel cut whose depth follows hold time (a 40% cut throttles, 100% severs, and neither can be undone); right-click-hold is a clamp, free and fully reversible but it spikes pressure upstream; G+drag grafts two vessels together, consuming eight seconds of the organism's whole growth budget; F drops nutrient, which raises local growth for twenty seconds and also feeds any rot within reach.
loop_10s: A pressure wave runs up the main trunk and you watch which junction takes it. Vessel 7-c has gone from locked phase to jitter — it is losing conviction and will be gone in about twenty-five seconds. Decision: clamp the trunk for three seconds to force flow through 7-c and re-commit it, at the price of a pressure spike upstream that may pop the thin wall you were nursing two minutes ago; or let 7-c die and accept that the eastern half of the mat now has exactly one route into it.
loop_2min: A demand cycle. Sink C ramps over ninety seconds. Vessels need roughly sixty seconds of sustained flow to thicken enough to carry a surge, so you must pre-thicken before you can possibly know which sink will surge — and you can only afford to prepare one route. The tell is that the organism senses it first: its own micro-flows drift toward a coming demand a few seconds before the demand is measurable at the sink. So the skill is reading your ward in order to predict the world, and the agonising choice is whether that faint drift toward C is real or is just the wake of your own last clamp.
mastery_loop: Understanding that adaptation is positive feedback — flux raises radius raises flux — so every intervention is amplified and every intervention is late. Learning atrophy and thickening time constants well enough to act on a system whose response is longer than your information horizon. Learning that a graft between vessels at similar pressure is nearly free while a graft across a pressure difference creates a shunt that steals the whole network within forty seconds. Learning the minimum clamping rhythm that keeps a cold spare alive for the least throughput cost, and learning to stop cutting.
tension: Efficiency versus survivability, made physical and visible. The organism always wants to become one fat trunk, which is beautiful and fast and dies to a single embolism. Every minute you spend buying redundancy shows up as a dimmer, slower, visibly unhappier network — you are paying a constant, legible cost for insurance you may never claim, against a system that quietly undoes your payments while you watch something else.
failure: Necrosis. A region starved for forty seconds dies, and dead tissue does not merely stop carrying — it becomes a rigid obstruction and a rot nucleus that creeps along contacting vessels at roughly one every fifteen seconds. Rot can only be stopped by amputating upstream, which costs more network, which starves more regions. The cascade is entirely legible ninety seconds before it kills you and usually unstoppable, because every remedy requires flow you no longer have. You spend the last minute of a failed session watching your own earlier efficiency arrive.
expression: The final geometry is a portrait of your policy. A braid keeper runs three medium parallel trunks with constant clamping labour: resilient, mediocre peak throughput, and a network that looks woven. A tourniquet keeper lets a single dominant tree form and manages it with violent periodic occlusions: high throughput, spectacular collapses, and a network that looks like a river delta. A grafter builds cross-connections the organism would never make and lives with the shunt risk. All three are viable and none looks like the others.
novice_vs_expert: A novice cuts what looks wrong — the congested vessel — and produces a worse congestion elsewhere ten seconds later, then cuts that too. They treat symptoms and their network is covered in scars. An expert acts far upstream, small and early, uses clamps almost exclusively because clamps are reversible and cuts are not, and does nothing at all for long stretches while the system settles. An expert's most common action is watching a jitter and choosing not to intervene.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The organism persists through the whole session, so a decision in minute three is still readable in minute twenty-five as a thick trunk you cannot now afford to lose. The difficulty does not scale by adding numbers; it scales because your ward has spent twenty-five minutes committing to a shape, and the shape is increasingly rigid, increasingly yours, and increasingly wrong for whatever the next demand cycle turns out to be.
why_not_an_existing_genre: Nothing is built, placed, bought or upgraded; there is no economy, no enemy and no expansion. The graph authors itself and the player can only argue with it after the fact. Logistics and pipe games hand you authorship of the network and ask you to optimise; this hands you a network that optimises itself and asks you to sabotage it correctly. The dominant action is restraint, and the antagonist is your ward's own competence.
falsifying_prototype: A 1200-edge network with Poiseuille flow solved by conjugate gradient on the graph Laplacian at 20 Hz, Tero-style radius adaptation, one clamp tool, a scripted demand curve, and atrophy plus necrosis. The test is narrow: does clamping the trunk to preserve a spare feel like a real decision — immediate visible cost, delayed uncertain benefit — or does it collapse into 'clamp everything on a rota'? If a fixed rota beats attentive play, it is a chore with a pulse effect and it is dead. Second test: can a tester point at a dying vessel and say why it is dying? If flow is not legible, none of the rest matters.
biggest_risks: The adaptation dynamics may have a very thin tuning band between trivially gameable and chaotic — the state where the organism appears to have convictions rather than moods is not guaranteed to exist at playable timescales. Legibility is the second risk: flow fields are genuinely hard to read, and if a player cannot see causation the whole thing degrades into pretty noise. Third, pacing: a system with sixty-second constants can read as waiting rather than tension, and the ten-second layer must carry real weight to prevent that.
feasibility_notes: Very comfortable. A sparse CG solve over 1-2k nodes with ~40 iterations at 20 Hz is trivial in plain JS with typed arrays, and the 60fps render is decoupled from it. Rendering: instanced capillary quads with an SDF line shader, additive glow, and pulses as a scrolling phase term — the visual identity comes entirely out of the simulation state (radius, flux, pressure, phase), so there is no art to make. Audio is procedural WebAudio: a bank of band-passed noise whose centre frequency tracks pressure, soft per-pulse transients so the network is audibly in or out of phase, and a low granular rasp for rot. Python only for a blue-noise seed layout of the initial mat.

name: Sounding
pitch: Black ice at dawn, seen from just above. You cannot see how thick it is. You strike it with a steel rod and listen: the return is a dispersive chirp — the high frequencies arrive first and the low ones lag — and the shape of that chirp tells you the thickness under you, the distance to the nearest flaw, and whether the water beneath is deep or shallow. Every strike also cracks the ice a little. You are out here to reach something and get back, and your ears are the only instrument you have.
central_verb: Sound — to strike and listen, which is simultaneously the only way to know anything and the main thing making the ice unsafe.
player_role: A practitioner reading a material by ear. The screen gives you almost nothing: a dark plane, wind scour, snow patches, the pale seams of refrozen leads, and a faint deformation ripple when you strike. The real channel is audio, synthesised from the actual geometry beneath you. Controls: WASD to move, with three gaits — walk, a shuffle that halves point load, and a crawl that spreads it over your whole body but is agonisingly slow; left-click strikes, with mouse distance choosing the standoff (striking far from your feet gives a weaker, muddier return but seeds no crack under you); hold right-click to put your ear to the ice, a continuous listen that reveals crack growth and distant booms but requires you to be prone and still; Q drops a marker. There is no map, no HUD thickness readout and no inventory.
loop_10s: At the edge of a snow patch you strike. The chirp comes back with a fast clean upsweep and a long ringing tail: thick ice, deep water. Two steps on you strike again and the upsweep is compressed, with a second quieter arrival about 90 ms later — a reflection off something roughly twelve metres ahead, bearing unknown. You now choose: strike again to bracket its bearing, which seeds another crack directly under your feet, or walk five metres sideways and strike from there, spending time you are also being charged for.
loop_2min: Crossing a lead — a refrozen seam running across your route. It sounds wrong along its whole length; the job is to find where it sounds least wrong and then commit. During the crossing you cannot strike, because the rod is stowed and you are moving, so you walk on the last reading you took and listen to the ice answer under your own weight in real time. If the answer changes halfway across, every option is bad and you have about two seconds.
mastery_loop: This is a genuinely perceptual skill and it trains like one. Within twenty or thirty minutes players stop reasoning about the chirp and start hearing thickness as a quality. Then the second layer: warm ice is duller and damps faster, so as the session ages your instrument degrades and you learn to take your risky readings early. Then the third: cracks you started earlier reflect your later strikes, so your own damage becomes an audible landmark. The expert navigates by the ruin they made on the way out.
tension: Knowledge costs integrity. The only way to be safe is to sound often, and sounding is precisely what makes the sheet unsafe. On top of that, the sun is warming the ice and the material is telling you so — the clock is not a number on screen, it is the fact that everything you strike is starting to sound dead.
failure: A through-crack under load. It is not instantaneous: you hear it start as a rising granular tear and you have roughly two seconds, and every option is bad. Run, which is maximum point load but the fastest exit. Drop flat, which is minimum load but leaves you six seconds from anywhere with the fracture still growing. Going through ends the run — and the sheet keeps your damage. The next attempt over the same ice begins with your old cracks still in it, still audible, still weak.
expression: Route and reading style, and they sound completely different. Some players sound sparsely and move boldly on thin inference, covering ground and accepting large uncertainty. Others sound densely and move along one narrow well-known corridor which they are slowly destroying with their own strikes, so that by run four the safest path they know is also the most damaged. The sheet accumulates a physical record of how you think.
novice_vs_expert: A novice strikes constantly and dies inside a crack network they built themselves, usually within sight of the shore. An expert strikes perhaps fifteen times in a whole run, mostly at long standoff, and reads the decaying tail of the chirp rather than its pitch — the tail carries the flaw information and the pitch only carries thickness. The expert also knows when a reading is good enough and stops asking.
why_still_good_after_an_hour: The perceptual skill keeps sharpening in a way that feels like real learning rather than progression, and the sheet keeps a permanent record of your past runs, so the environment gets harder in exactly the places you have used most. Push the objective further out and the acoustic problem compounds: readings taken three minutes ago in colder, stiffer ice are now optimistic by an amount you have to estimate.
why_not_an_existing_genre: The primary information channel is a synthesised physical signal rather than a user interface, and the core act of play is measurement — where measurement is itself the hazard. There is no combat, no crafting, no inventory, no map. Survival games ask you to gather and defend; this asks you to infer, and charges you for inferring. The closest honest comparison is a sonar operator, and that is a job, not a genre.
falsifying_prototype: A 60x60 m sheet with a thickness heightfield and a handful of flaws; a dispersive delay-network acoustic model producing returns computed from real geometry, never from canned samples; walking with a load field and one crack-propagation rule. The decisive test: give testers no visual thickness cue at all, let them play freely for fifteen minutes, then ask them to pick the thicker of two spots by ear alone, twenty times. If they cannot beat chance convincingly, the signal is not learnable and the entire concept is dead — no amount of art or pacing rescues it. Secondary test: does a rising tear give enough warning to make the two-second choice feel like a decision rather than a coin flip?
biggest_risks: The audio must be legible, not merely physically motivated — honest flexural dispersion may be too subtle, or every location may sound the same, and the fix (exaggerating) risks turning a real perceptual skill into a cartoon one. Accessibility is a genuine problem: a game whose core channel is audio excludes players, and the visual fallback has to be an honestly degraded instrument rather than a cheat. There is a hard CPU ceiling on an audio-rate waveguide network in a single AudioWorklet. And the tension can collapse into 'stand still and never strike', which needs a clock the player believes in.
feasibility_notes: Well matched to the stack, and the acoustics are the interesting part rather than the risky part: flexural dispersion is mathematically an allpass, so a graph of allpass-chained delay lines with scattering junctions at cracks and edges produces real chirps almost for free — around 200 junctions in one AudioWorklet is affordable. Physics: a 256x256 thickness heightfield, a Winkler-foundation stress solve run only on a 64x64 patch around the player, and cracks as polylines grown by a stress criterion. Rendering: an SDF of the crack network for the luminous seams, thickness driving a subsurface tint, snow from two octaves of noise, wind scour from a flow-warped noise field — no authored art anywhere, and Python/PIL only for noise and blue-noise lookup textures. Comfortably 60fps.
